common_name: Queen Lime Blotch Zinnia (AAS-Winning Lime-Green Zinnia with Rose Center Blotch)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 4-5 weeks earlier for an earlier first flush; give full sun and generous spacing for strong air circulation.

directions: Queen Lime Blotch extends the popular Queen Lime line with a muted chartreuse-green flower marked by a distinct rose-purple blotch at the base of each petal ring, an unusual two-tone effect that set it apart enough to earn an All-America Selections award. Plants grow tall and vigorous on strong stems, producing a steady supply of long-lasting blooms prized by cut-flower growers and florists for their unusual coloring. Deadhead or harvest regularly to keep new buds forming through summer, and space plants generously to reduce powdery mildew in humid weather.

common_name: Benary's Giant Bright Pink Zinnia (Large-Flowered Cut-Flower Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4-5 weeks earlier; tall Benary's Giant stems benefit from sturdy support netting in cutting-garden rows.

directions: Bright Pink is one of the single-color selections within the Benary's Giant line, producing fully double, dahlia-like flowers up to five inches across in a clear, vivid pink on tall, exceptionally strong stems. Breeders bred the series specifically for commercial cut-flower production, and the uniform color selections like Bright Pink let growers plan single-hue bunches rather than relying on the mixed-color strain. Weekly harvesting encourages continuous branching and bloom production right up to frost, and the sturdy stems hold up well in buckets and vases without wilting.

common_name: Benary's Giant Carmine Zinnia (Large-Flowered Cut-Flower Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4-5 weeks earlier; support rows with netting as plants reach full height.

directions: Carmine is the deep, rich red-pink single-color selection in the Benary's Giant series, carrying the same oversized fully double blooms and tall, thick stems the series is known for among commercial and hobby cut-flower growers. The saturated carmine tone reads darker and warmer than the series' Bright Pink or Salmon Rose, making it a favorite for bold bouquet mixes. Harvest when the outer petal rows have fully opened for the longest vase life, and keep plants picked regularly to sustain branching and flower production through the season.

common_name: Benary's Giant Deep Red Zinnia (Large-Flowered Cut-Flower Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4-5 weeks earlier; stake or net cutting rows as stems reach their full height.

directions: Deep Red delivers the darkest, most velvety red in the Benary's Giant lineup, with the same fully double, four-to-five-inch flowers and heavy, non-branching-to-moderately-branching stems bred for cut-flower rows. Its intense color holds well in full summer heat without fading or bleaching, a trait the series is bred for alongside disease tolerance. Pick stems as soon as the center disk florets begin to show for the best vase life, and keep up a weekly harvest schedule to push continued flower production.

common_name: Benary's Giant Lilac Zinnia (Large-Flowered Cut-Flower Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4-5 weeks earlier; generous spacing and netting support keep tall stems straight for cutting.

directions: Lilac offers a soft, cool lavender-purple tone that stands apart from the warmer reds, oranges, and pinks elsewhere in the Benary's Giant series, giving growers a pastel option with the same giant double flower form and sturdy stems. The muted color blends easily into mixed bouquets and softer floral palettes, which has made it a popular addition to specialty cut-flower rows. Deadhead or harvest spent stems promptly to keep plants branching and producing new buds through the heat of summer.

common_name: Benary's Giant Orange Zinnia (Large-Flowered Cut-Flower Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4-5 weeks earlier; stake or net rows as plants approach full height.

directions: Orange brings a bright, saturated tangerine tone to the Benary's Giant series, with the same large, fully double flowers and vigorous, upright plants that make the series a cut-flower-industry standard. Its bold color pairs readily with the series' Golden Yellow and Scarlet selections for warm-toned bouquet mixes. Harvest stems in the cooler part of the day once flowers are fully open, and keep plants well watered and regularly picked to maintain production over a long summer season.

common_name: Double Zahara Strawberry Zinnia (Fully Double Rose-Pink Landscape Zinnia)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably warm; Double Zahara's compact, mounding habit suits beds, borders, and containers without staking.

directions: Double Zahara Strawberry adds a clear rose-pink to the fully double side of the Zahara landscape series, covering compact, well-branched plants with two-inch blooms that keep their shape better in rain and humidity than many old-fashioned double zinnias. Like the rest of the Zahara line, it was bred for strong resistance to the leaf-spotting and powdery mildew diseases that plague traditional Zinnia elegans in humid climates, making it reliable for mass bedding without constant deadheading. Plants flower continuously from late spring to frost with minimal care beyond routine watering during dry spells.

common_name: Chief Carmine Celosia (Large Crested Cockscomb Cut Flower)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature and transplant after nights stay reliably above 60°F; Chief series plants grow tall and benefit from rich, well-drained soil.

directions: Chief Carmine produces the dense, velvety, brain-like crests typical of crested cockscomb in a bright carmine-red, held on strong, uniform stems bred for commercial cut-flower production. The large two-to-seven-inch blooms hold their color and shape well both fresh in arrangements and air-dried for everlasting displays. Plants are heat-tolerant and largely pest-free, performing best with consistent moisture and full sun through the growing season, and harvesting regularly encourages continued flowering until frost.

common_name: Chief Gold Celosia (Large Crested Cockscomb Cut Flower)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant after nights stay reliably above 60°F; do not cover seed, as light aids germination.

directions: Chief Gold carries the same dense, convoluted crest shape as the rest of the Chief series but in a sunny golden-yellow that reads as a warm highlight color in mixed cut-flower bunches. Plants grow notably tall and sturdy-stemmed for a cockscomb type, a trait the series was bred for to suit field and greenhouse cut-flower production. Blooms are long-lasting fresh and dry cleanly for everlasting arrangements, and full sun with even moisture through summer keeps the crests full-sized and well colored.

common_name: Chief Persimmon Celosia (Large Crested Cockscomb Cut Flower)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant after nights stay reliably above 60°F; strong stems make Chief Persimmon well suited to field cut-flower rows.

directions: Chief Persimmon bears vivid orange-red crested blooms on the same strong, uniform stems that make the Chief series a standard choice for commercial cut-flower growers producing cockscomb for fresh and dried markets. The vibrant persimmon-orange tone bridges the series' red and gold selections, adding a warm accent to mixed bouquets. Give plants full sun and steady moisture through summer, and harvest stems as the crests reach full size for the longest display life whether used fresh or hung to dry.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Bombay types were bred for uniform greenhouse and field production of cut flowers.

directions: Bombay Pink produces the flattened, fan-shaped, coral-like crests characteristic of the Bombay series in a clear, bright pink, a color that has remained the series' most widely grown shade since its introduction. Plants are compact and uniform, bred specifically for reliable cut-flower and bedding production rather than the oversized brain-like crests of older cockscomb strains. The sturdy, velvety heads hold their color well both as fresh cuts and when air-dried, and full sun with even moisture keeps crests developing at full size.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 60°F; grow in full sun with consistent moisture for the fullest crests.

directions: Bombay Red carries deep, velvety red fan-shaped crests on compact, well-branched plants, part of a series bred for the floral and bedding trade as a fast, uniform alternative to traditional rounded cockscomb. Its coral-like, ridged flower heads are long-lasting both as fresh cut flowers and when dried for everlasting arrangements, holding their rich color with little fading. Plants perform best in full sun with regular watering through summer heat, and prompt removal of spent heads keeps new ones forming.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Pink Candle flowers notably earlier than most wheat celosia selections.

directions: Pink Candle bears slender, upright, wheat-like flower spikes in a deep pink brushed with silvery highlights, maturing to a more muted rose-mauve as blooms age through the season. It was selected for notably early flowering compared with other wheat celosia strains, giving cutting gardens a head start on this slow-to-bloom type. The tapering spikes are excellent fresh in arrangements and dry cleanly for everlasting bouquets, and plants tolerate heat and drier soil better than the plumed or crested celosia types.

common_name: Kelos Fire Orange Celosia (Compact Flame-Shaped Plumed Celosia)
scientific_name: Celosia argentea var. plumosa 'Kelos Fire Orange'

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Kelos Fire types branch freely and hold their flame-shaped plumes well into fall.

directions: Kelos Fire Orange produces neon-bright orange, flame-shaped plumes on compact, well-branched plants bred for season-long color in beds, borders, and containers rather than cutting. The Kelos Fire line was developed for vivid, saturated color that holds through summer heat and into cool fall weather without fading or collapsing. Plants need little maintenance beyond full sun and consistent moisture, flowering continuously from early summer through the first hard frost.

common_name: Kelos Fire Purple Celosia (Compact Flame-Shaped Plumed Celosia)
scientific_name: Celosia argentea var. plumosa 'Kelos Fire Purple'

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 60°F; this rich purple selection pairs well with the Kelos Fire series' warmer tones in mixed plantings.

directions: Kelos Fire Purple offers a deep, rich purple take on the series' signature flame-shaped plumes, standing out from the more typical reds, oranges, and pinks found in most plumed celosia. As with its Kelos Fire siblings, the compact, uniform habit and heat tolerance make it well suited to mass bedding and container displays that need reliable color through late summer and fall. It requires only full sun and even moisture to perform, with no deadheading needed to maintain a long, continuous bloom season.

common_name: Double Click Bicolor Pink Cosmos (Fully Double Pink-and-White Cut Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed in average, well-drained soil, or start indoors 3-4 weeks earlier; thin seedlings once established and avoid overly rich soil.

directions: Double Click Bicolor Pink produces frilly, double and semi-double blooms with a variable wash of dark pink over white, so that no two flowers on a plant look quite alike, from nearly all-white centers brushed with blush to deep pink edges fading toward a paler base. Like other Double Click selections, it was bred to hold a high percentage of fully double flowers from seed, unlike the single daisy form typical of most cosmos. Tall, wiry stems make it a dependable cut flower, and frequent harvesting or deadheading keeps plants blooming from summer into fall in lean, well-drained soil.

common_name: Double Click White Cosmos (Fully Double White Cut Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed in average, well-drained soil, or start indoors 3-4 weeks earlier; thin seedlings once established.

directions: Double Click White gives the Double Click strain's large, frilly, fully double blooms in pure white, resembling small double dahlias rather than the flat single daisy form of a typical cosmos. Tall, airy, well-branched plants hold up well as cut flowers, and the clean white color blends easily into mixed bouquets or stands alone in an all-white planting. Cosmos of this type flower best in lean, well-drained soil with modest watering, since overly rich conditions encourage lush foliage and floppy stems at the expense of bloom.
